extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media critics, and general readers interested in explainer/newsroom practices
extracted.subtask_description: A critical checklist for assessing or producing 'explainer' (explanatory) journalism — pieces that aim to make complex news topics accessible to general readers. Focuses on definition, methods (data/visuals/aggregation), tone, expertise, scope limits, bias, and market incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — clarity: distilling complexity for ordinary readers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Explainer journalism" describes a model in which complex news topics — including technical issues like the federal budget — are boiled down for the ordinary reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genre's emblematic template is to start at square one and present the core idea simply so non-specialists can understand. Examples include Wonkblog and Vox. The fundamental metric: does the piece make a complicated topic graspable without introducing significant error?

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-versus-explainer distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer journalism is related to but distinct from data journalism; publications like FiveThirtyEight emphasize data-driven analysis, while Vox-style explainers prioritize clear context and exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the piece is primarily narrative/contextual explanation or structured around original data analysis; hybrid work is common. Consider whether data-visualization is used substantively or merely decoratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of data visualization and explanatory visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainers often incorporate visualized data—sometimes reduced to the 'X, explained in one chart' trope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals should illuminate rather than oversimplify or serve as clickbait. Check that charts are accurate, labeled, sourced, and genuinely add explanatory value rather than substituting for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and traffic incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Many institutions adopt the explainer model for its traffic potential; successful practitioners (e.g., Ezra Klein, Nate Silver) have driven imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to formulaic, attention-seeking tropes born of traffic-chasing. Distinguish commercially motivated packaging from genuine editorial judgment about reader needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filling an informational gap / providing context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainers claim to 'fill a hole' in journalism by raising readers' level of knowledge and supplying essential context readers lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the piece genuinely increases readers' understanding (by supplying context, background, and connections) rather than merely summarizing or repeating headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter expertise and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Many explainer outlets rely on young generalist writers, some with little or no traditional reporting experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider author credentials and reporting background. Complex topics handled by non-specialists (especially without reporting time or primary-source reporting) risk missing nuance or factual subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original reporting versus aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer sites often aggregate data and analysis from other sources to provide context for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the balance between original reporting/analysis and aggregation. Aggregation should be transparent about sources and add synthesis or interpretation rather than just repackaging others' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of topic scope for the explainer format
rubrics_metrics.description: Some issues are too complex to be succinctly and fairly explained to lay audiences by non-specialist journalists working on deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the topic can be responsibly simplified. For subjects with deep technical, legal, or scientific complexity, a short explainer may mislead; prefer longer-form reporting or expert collaboration where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone — respectfulness versus condescension
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer journalism is at special risk of adopting an intentionally dumbed-down, cloyingly didactic tone that can feel condescending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good explainers 'meet readers where they are' without talking down. Measure tone for humility, clarity, and absence of patronizing language; avoid analogies or simplifications that infantilize the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political neutrality and ideological framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer outlets and staff backgrounds influence perspective; empiricism and data-driven framing can align with particular political tendencies (the piece notes that empiricism in America currently skews liberal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims and framing for implicit ideological assumptions. Transparency about worldview and sourcing helps; readers should be able to detect if empiricism is being used as a proxy for a partisan stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience positioning and socio-demographic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer journalism tends to adopt the worldview of the college-educated, highly Internet-conscious, socially liberal upper middle-class and present those concerns as broadly 'understanding' the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider who the piece is written for and which perspectives are centered or excluded. Good explainers are aware of demographic blind spots and avoid presenting a parochial perspective as universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of distortion from simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre 'downplays the distorting effects that inevitably result from trying to portray an issue in "simple" terms that anybody can understand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for omissions that materially change meaning, overgeneralizations, or false certainties introduced by simplification. Favor qualifiers where warranted and signpost complexity rather than erase it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time/deadline constraints affecting depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer writers often work on deadlines, which limits how deeply they can probe complicated topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for reporting time and depth in assessing quality. Fast-turn explainers should be transparent about limits and avoid overstating certainty when reporting was constrained by time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality variability, editorial humility, and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainer work can be 'accessible, informative, usually smart, and often entertaining' but also 'done poorly'; the piece includes a published correction as an example of editorial correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial standards: fact-checking, source transparency, and willingness to correct errors. High-quality explainer outlets show institutional practices for corrections and accountability.
